assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework with nominal rigidities is the workhorse of modern monetary policy analysis and practice. It has changed both academic macroeconomics and central-bank thinking, and it has a broad, durable record of influence. I rate this the strongest case on the list.
assessment.attribution: Calvo (time-dependent pricing), Taylor (staggered contracts and the policy rule) and Woodford (the micro-founded, welfare-based policy synthesis) are the clearest foundational credits. Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets made large estimation and policy-model contributions. Choosing three means leaving out others with real claims, which is the main attribution difficulty.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature. The key papers date from the 1980s to the early 2000s, and their influence has been confirmed through several macro cycles, including the financial crisis and the inflation episode after 2021.
uncertainties: Three-name limit forces hard choices among Gali, Gertler, Christiano and Eichenbaum.
Some of the field's critics argue the framework was tested by the 2008 and 2021-22 episodes, though the tools survived and were extended.
Calvo's age and the committee's timing preferences.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work formalises how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy and development. It has built a coherent field of modern political economics, with theory and empirical work that others have taken up widely.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini have the clearest joint programme (constitutions, electoral rules and policy outcomes). Besley's work on state capacity and accountability is closely linked to theirs. The trio is a coherent group, though it overlaps with other political-economy contributions, such as Acemoglu-Robinson, which the Prize has already recognised.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The core contributions date from the 1990s and 2000s and have been confirmed by a large literature.
uncertainties: Persson is an institutional colleague at IIES and a former committee chair. I disclose this without treating it as a reason to rank higher or lower.
The Prize has recently recognised related institutions research, which could reduce the marginal case.
Whether the committee sees the programme as a single discovery or as several.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Misallocation across firms gave macroeconomics and development economics a quantitative way to explain cross-country income differences. It changed how researchers think about productivity gaps and how they measure them.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) gave the central measurement framework. Restuccia and Rogerson (2008) is the closely parallel theoretical contribution, and Rogerson is not on the credited list, which makes the credit question harder. Restuccia is credited for his agricultural and development applications.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature. The key papers are about 15-17 years old and have strong citation records, though the measurement approach faces ongoing critiques.
uncertainties: Measurement concerns (the role of mismeasured distortions and heterogeneity) remain active.
The Restuccia-Rogerson parallel may complicate any three-name selection.
How much of the policy evidence is causal remains open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamic panel GMM estimators are used in a very large share of applied empirical work across fields. They are a clear case of methodological work with broad applied impact.
assessment.attribution: The Arellano-Bond (1991) difference GMM estimator and the Arellano-Bover and Blundell-Bond system GMM estimators are clearly attributable. Anderson-Hsiao, Holtz-Eakin, Newey and Rosen, and Chamberlain are precursors that may complicate credit.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with several decades of use. Known weaknesses, such as instrument proliferation and weak instruments, have been documented and handled in practice.
uncertainties: The committee may prefer a methods prize built around other themes.
Credit for Blundell is also tied to his labour and consumption work, which could blur the framing of the case.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Top-income and wealth-distribution series reshaped the empirical study of inequality and public debate. Their combination of tax data and long historical series has become a standard approach and has influenced the theory of taxation and distribution.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez (2003) created the core top-income series. Zucman's contributions on offshore wealth and distributional national accounts are recent and extend the programme. Atkinson, who is deceased, is also a precursor of this work.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature. The early series are about 20 years old, but the interpretive claims (such as r>g) remain debated and parts of the measurement are contested.
uncertainties: Debate over the measurement of top shares and the interpretation of capital-income dynamics.
Zucman's work is newer, so I leave him off the proposed list.
Distance between the descriptive contribution and the causal or theoretical content.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bayesian persuasion and information design give a general framework for how a designer chooses what information to reveal. It has spread across theory, mechanism design, finance, regulation and applied work. The framework is conceptually clean and has real intellectual depth.
assessment.attribution: Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011) are the originators of Bayesian persuasion. Bergemann and Morris developed the broader information-design and Bayes correlated equilibrium approach. Naming three leaves out Bergemann, whose claim is strong, and earlier cheap-talk and disclosure work (Crawford-Sobel, Milgrom, Aumann-Maschler) is also relevant precursor credit.
assessment.maturity: Intermediate. The core results are about 15 years old, the theory is established, and applications are growing, but the empirical and policy confirmation is thinner than for the top-ranked candidates.
uncertainties: Whether the committee considers it mature enough.
Overlap with prior recognition of information economics and mechanism design.
Choice among Bergemann, Morris and Kamenica-Gentzkow.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Task-based and trade-shock analyses of labour demand explain wage polarisation and the distributional effects of technology and globalisation. The work is influential in academic and policy debate and is central to a first-order economic question.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Katz and Hanson (with Dorn on the China shock) are the central names. Acemoglu and Restrepo, who have also developed task models, are not on this list, and the Levy-Murnane and Katz-Murphy contributions overlap with the credited group, so credit is spread across several groups.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature. The core work is 10-20 years old, but the long-run effects of trade shocks and automation are still being revised.
uncertainties: Competing task-model credits outside the listed names.
Debate over how much the China-shock evidence generalises.
Partial overlap with the inequality and technology theme.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Uncertainty shocks and policy-uncertainty measurement brought a new channel for business cycles and investment into macroeconomics, supported by a measurable index. The work has been very influential in macro and policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: Bloom (2009) is the central macro contribution on uncertainty shocks. Baker, Bloom and Davis (2016) created the policy-uncertainty index. Davis is credited mainly for the index and for his earlier work on job flows. Bloom also appears on the management-practices candidate, so credit would need to be compared across the two cases.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature. The work is influential, but the identification of causal effects is debated, and the ranking leaves room for older, more settled contributions.
uncertainties: Causality and identification of uncertainty effects remain debated.
Overlap with other work on uncertainty and real options.
Bloom's credit spans two longlist entries.
